newsitem.title: UK: Britain says hardline Russia NATO stance is ploy.
newsitem.headline: Britain says hardline Russia NATO stance is ploy.

text.p: A senior British official on Wednesday played down recent Russian hardline comments on NATO expansion, saying they were a negotiating ploy to gain as many concessions from the Alliance as possible.

The official, speaking on the grounds of anonymity, also said it was highly unlikely Turkey would carry out its threat to block NATO enlargement unless it were given the green light to start negotiating for European Union membership.
Russia has consistently said NATO expansion would threaten its security. On Tuesday it stepped up the pressure by saying enlargement would undermine President Boris Yeltsin's already shaky position.

"I think Russia would like to extract a price for enlargement. They know they can't stop it, so this is an entirely logical tactic," the official told reporters. "The West has to identify serious propositions which Russia can accept.
NATO has made clear nothing will stop it from holding a summit in July to decide which former Warsaw Pact states should be invited to start membership talks.

The favourites are the Czech Republic, Hungary and Poland. "If Moscow continues to say expansion won't happen up until the very moment it does, that would represent a failure of Russian diplomacy," said the official.
Diplomats in Paris said French President Jacques Chirac had floated the idea of a five-power summit to establish the broad lines of a deal that could let Moscow accept NATO expansion.

The official said the key elements of such a deal were likely to be assurances that nuclear weapons would not be deployed on the soil of new member states and a new treaty on Conventional Forces in Europe taking greater account of Russia's security needs.

The official also said new permanent consultation mechanisms between the two sides could be set up, a so-called "co-decision" making process, but poured cold water on the idea that Russia could ever be given a veto on important alliance business.

"There may be some modest area (of joint talks) where we can present it as consultations, but this will be largely cosmetic, if the truth be told. I do not see it as likely we'll accept co-decision on matters of real importance," the official said.
Another headache for NATO is the increasingly irritated stance of Turkey, which is angry that its bid to join the EU is still on the back-burner decades after it first applied.
The EU says it first wants to see progress on human rights, the Kurdish issue and Turkey's various disputes with Greece, especially over the divided island of Cyprus.
"I don't think they'll veto NATO expansion. This is a negotiating position. I don't think they can single-handedly stop it," the official said.
"It would be extremely silly for them to insist that for NATO expansion to go ahead they must join the EU next year."
